subject: English
title: Three Days to See
hook: If you could see for only three days, what would you really look at?

characters.name: Rahul
characters.role: thoughtful boy who loves noticing things

characters.name: His grandmother
characters.role: blind since youth, but sees life differently

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: his friend who thinks sight is everything

slides.title: Three Days to See
slides.storyContext: What if you had only three days to see the world? Would you rush to see everything, or look deeply at what matters most?

image.alt: Three Days to See — Three Days to See

slides.title: Grandmother's Question
slides.storyContext: Rahul and his friend Meera visit Rahul's grandmother in Varanasi. Meera complains about not having enough time to see the ghats, the temples, and the riverside. Grandmother laughs gently and asks: 'If you had only three days of sight in your whole life, what would you truly want to see?' Meera is stumped. But Grandmother's question makes Rahul think deeply.
slides.inSimpleWords: A wise grandmother makes two young people question what they really value.

image.alt: Grandmother's Question — Three Days to See

slides.title: Understanding the Author's Purpose

points.label: What is it?
points.text: Why did the author write this piece? To entertain? To teach? To make you think?

points.label: In 'Three Days to See'
points.text: The author (based on Helen Keller's essay) wants us to see how we take sight for granted and waste it on unimportant things.

example.problem: Why does the grandmother ask this question instead of just scolding Meera for complaining?
example.solution: The author wants us to learn through reflection, not rules. By making Meera imagine losing sight, she (and the reader) discovers what sight really means. This is more powerful than being told 'sight is precious.'

slides.inSimpleWords: The reason an author writes—to teach, move, or change how you think.

image.alt: Understanding the Author's Purpose — Three Days to See

slides.title: The Power of Questions to Change Thinking

points.label: A good question
points.text: Doesn't have an easy answer. It makes you stop and really think.

points.label: Grandmother's question
points.text: 'What would you see if you had three days?' is not about Varanasi or temples. It's about what Meera truly values.

example.problem: If Grandmother had said, 'Stop wasting time, look at what matters,' would Meera learn the same way?
example.solution: No. A direct command might make Meera defensive. But asking 'What would YOU choose to see?' makes her think for herself. Questions are more powerful than orders.

slides.inSimpleWords: A real question makes you think deeper than any answer could.

image.alt: The Power of Questions to Change Thinking — Three Days to See

slides.title: Appreciating the Ordinary

points.label: The idea
points.text: The most important things to see are often right in front of us—a parent's face, a child's smile, sunlight on water.

points.label: Meera's mistake
points.text: She wanted to check off famous sights, but if sight was leaving forever, a stranger's temple wouldn't matter as much as her grandmother's hands.

example.problem: On Day One, what would you actually choose to see if sight was ending?
example.solution: Most people say: faces of loved ones, their home, a place that makes them feel safe. Not famous landmarks. This shows that we need to pay attention to small, ordinary beauty NOW, not wait until it's gone.

slides.inSimpleWords: The everyday things around you are more precious than famous places.

image.alt: Appreciating the Ordinary — Three Days to See

slides.title: Different Ways of Seeing

points.label: Sight vs. vision
points.text: Sight is the ability to see with eyes. Vision is the ability to understand and value what you see.

points.label: Grandmother's example
points.text: Though blind since youth, Grandmother 'sees' Meera's heart through her complaints. She sees what matters.

example.problem: Can someone blind truly 'see' better than someone with eyes?
example.solution: Yes. Grandmother uses her other senses—hearing tone of voice, feeling emotions, remembering. She 'sees' people's real needs because she pays full attention. Having eyes doesn't mean you truly see.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real seeing means understanding and paying attention, not just using eyes.

image.alt: Different Ways of Seeing — Three Days to See

slides.title: Perspective: Three Days Lesson

points.label: Day One
points.text: See the people you love most—family, close friends. Their faces, expressions, the tiny things that make them unique.

points.label: Day Two
points.text: See the world in motion—a marketplace, children playing, farmers in fields, seasons changing.

points.label: Day Three
points.text: See beauty in silence—nature, art, your own country, the sky at different times.

example.problem: What would your three days look like?
example.solution: Answers vary, but good answers prioritize people over places, feeling over collecting experiences, and noticing small details (not checking off a list). The point is: what would REALLY matter if you lost it soon?

slides.inSimpleWords: If we had limited time to see, we'd notice what we usually ignore.

image.alt: Perspective: Three Days Lesson — Three Days to See

slides.title: A Real Moment: Meera's Realization
slides.storyContext: After three days with Grandmother, Meera sits quietly by the Ghat at sunset. She notices: the way light falls on her grandmother's weathered hands as they feed pigeons, the exact blue-gray of the Ganges, a child's laugh echoing off stone. She whispers to Rahul, 'I've been looking at the temples, but I haven't really SEEN anything.' Rahul says, 'Neither had I until Grandmother asked.'

example.problem: What changed for Meera?
example.solution: She stopped collecting sights (temples, ghats, famous spots) and started actually observing—noticing light, color, emotion, connection. She learned that seeing is an act of love and attention, not a checklist.

slides.inSimpleWords: When we slow down and really look, the world becomes beautiful.

image.alt: A Real Moment: Meera's Realization — Three Days to See

slides.title: Your Three Days of Sight
slides.storyContext: Imagine you had three days of sight (or sound, or any sense) left. Write a plan for how you'd spend those days. Don't list tourist spots—list moments, people, and small details you never want to forget.

example.problem: Plan your three days of sight.
example.solution: Example: 'Day 1: I'd look at my mother's face for hours, then my little brother sleeping. Day 2: I'd watch farmers in the fields near my village, and children playing cricket at sunset. Day 3: I'd sit in my room and really look at everything I own, every corner, as if saying goodbye.' (Any genuine, detailed answer showing priorities beyond famous places is correct.)

slides.inSimpleWords: What would you truly want to see if time were running out?

image.alt: Your Three Days of Sight — Three Days to See

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: **Author's purpose**: Why they wrote it—often to make us think differently about life.
**Power of questions**: A question can teach more than an answer.
**Ordinary is precious**: Small daily moments matter more than famous sights.
**Real seeing is vision**: Having eyes isn't the same as truly observing and understanding.
**Perspective matters**: Imagining loss helps us value what we have now.
**Attention is love**: When we really look at someone or something, we show we care.

slides.inSimpleWords: The essay teaches us to see the world with fresh eyes, noticing what matters most.

image.alt: What We Learned — Three Days to See

subject: English
title: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle
hook: A doctor who speaks to animals learns that they have their own wisdom and problems.

characters.name: Dr. Dolittle
characters.role: humble veterinary doctor who listens to animals

characters.name: Arun
characters.role: village boy who brings injured animals to the doctor

characters.name: The parrot Rama
characters.role: wise, talkative, and critical of humans

slides.title: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle
slides.storyContext: What if animals could speak? What would they tell us about how we treat them?

image.alt: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: A Doctor Like No Other
slides.storyContext: In a small Indian town, Dr. Dolittle isn't famous or rich. But animals seek him out. A parrot with a broken wing comes to his door. A stray dog leads him to a cat stuck in a tree. When children ask, 'How do you know what to do?' Dr. Dolittle says, 'I listen. Not with my ears alone—I watch, I pay attention, and I imagine what they must feel.' The parrot Rama becomes his harshest critic and truest friend.
slides.inSimpleWords: A doctor heals animals by listening to them as if they were his friends.

image.alt: A Doctor Like No Other — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: Dialogue: Words That Show Character

points.label: What is it?
points.text: When characters speak in a story, what they say and HOW they say it tells you who they are.

points.label: Dr. Dolittle's style
points.text: He speaks gently, asks questions, and admits when he doesn't know. This shows he's humble and curious.

points.label: Rama's style
points.text: The parrot speaks sharply and criticizes. This shows he's intelligent but also frustrated with humans.

example.problem: When Rama says, 'Humans are clumsy, loud, and careless,' what does this tell us?
example.solution: Rama has seen humans hurt or ignore animals. His sharp words come from pain and watching injustice. Good dialogue doesn't just move the plot—it reveals the character's history and values.

slides.inSimpleWords: What characters say and how they say it shows who they really are.

image.alt: Dialogue: Words That Show Character — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: Point of View: Seeing Through Animal Eyes

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: The story could be told from a human's view ('I helped the bird') or an animal's ('This towering stranger caught me, but his hands were gentle').

points.label: The effect
points.text: Telling it from the animal's perspective makes us feel what they feel—fear, relief, trust—instead of just admiring the doctor.

example.problem: If we heard only the doctor's view, what would we miss?
example.solution: We'd miss the animal's terror and confusion, the effort it takes for them to trust, and the wisdom in their silence. Switching perspective makes us empathize with creatures we usually ignore.

slides.inSimpleWords: Seeing the story through the animal's eyes helps us understand their feelings.

image.alt: Point of View: Seeing Through Animal Eyes — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: Conflict: Animals vs. Human Carelessness

points.label: External conflict
points.text: The animal is injured, hungry, or lost because humans trapped it, hit it with a cart, or took its home.

points.label: Internal conflict (human side)
points.text: Dr. Dolittle struggles between helping individual animals and knowing he can't save them all. He's sad but keeps trying.

points.label: The real conflict
points.text: Humans don't know animals have complex feelings and needs. The doctor's mission is to bridge that gap.

example.problem: Why is Rama so angry? Isn't Dr. Dolittle one of the good humans?
example.solution: Rama is angry because one kind doctor doesn't fix the whole system. Hundreds of animals suffer daily while most humans stay blind. Rama's anger is justified—it shows the author takes animal suffering seriously.

slides.inSimpleWords: The real fight in the story is between human ignorance and animal suffering.

image.alt: Conflict: Animals vs. Human Carelessness — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: Symbolism: What Do the Animals Represent?

points.label: What is symbolism?
points.text: A character, object, or event that stands for a bigger idea (e.g., a bird = freedom, a storm = chaos).

points.label: In this story
points.text: Each animal the doctor helps represents a real human problem he could solve if he paid attention.

points.label: The broken-winged parrot
points.text: Symbolizes a voice silenced by human cruelty—but healing gives it back.

example.problem: Why does the author include so many different animals—birds, dogs, cats, insects?
example.solution: Each one has a different kind of suffering and different wisdom. Together they show that we're surrounded by beings who need help and have lessons to teach us. No single animal tells the whole story.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each animal in the story represents a real problem humans need to solve.

image.alt: Symbolism: What Do the Animals Represent? — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: Empathy: Feeling What Others Feel

points.label: What is it?
points.text: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another creature, even if very different from you.

points.label: Dr. Dolittle's power
points.text: He doesn't really 'speak' to animals in words. He observes, remembers, imagines their suffering, and acts on it. That's empathy.

example.problem: A hungry stray dog chews garbage. An angry person chases it away. How would Dr. Dolittle think differently?
example.solution: He'd imagine: 'This dog is starving. It's not choosing to be a nuisance—it's surviving. Instead of anger, I should provide food.' He moves from judgment to understanding.

slides.inSimpleWords: Empathy means putting yourself in another being's place and understanding their needs.

image.alt: Empathy: Feeling What Others Feel — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: A Full Episode: The Parrot's Lesson
slides.storyContext: Rama arrives with a wounded wing, barely alive. As Dr. Dolittle heals him over weeks, the parrot slowly speaks about his cage, the child who mistreated him, and the freedom he once knew. When Rama can finally fly again, he pauses at the window. 'You're unlike other humans,' he says. 'But don't mistake kindness for justice. True help means letting me return to the wild, not keeping me as a grateful pet.' Dr. Dolittle opens the window. Rama flies free, but visits every morning to share news of the forest.

example.problem: Why doesn't Rama stay with Dr. Dolittle, even though he's safe and loved?
example.solution: True empathy means respecting what others actually want, not what we think is best for them. Rama wants freedom and wildness. Keeping him 'safe' would be a gentler cage. The doctor understands this and sets him free—that is real love.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real kindness sometimes means letting go and respecting freedom.

image.alt: A Full Episode: The Parrot's Lesson — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: An Animal's Story
slides.storyContext: Think of an animal you've seen—a cow at a village fair, a street dog, a bird at your window, an insect in your kitchen. Write a short paragraph from that animal's point of view. What did it see, feel, and need from humans?

example.problem: Tell an animal's experience in its own voice.
example.solution: Example (a street dog): 'Every morning I search the same three alleys for scraps. The children sometimes kick, sometimes throw me food. I don't hate them—I just want to eat and find a warm place to sleep. When the old man sits by the wall, he doesn't chase me. That's a good day.' (Any genuine perspective from an animal's point of view, showing need and limited understanding of humans, is correct.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Imagine being an animal and describe what the world looks like to you.

image.alt: An Animal's Story — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: **Dialogue reveals character**: What someone says and how they say it shows who they are.
**Point of view matters**: Telling the story from the animal's view makes us empathize more.
**Conflict is often deeper**: Not just about fixing a problem, but about changing hearts.
**Symbolism teaches**: Each character can represent a bigger human truth.
**Empathy is action**: Understanding is good, but acting on it matters more.
**Respect freedom**: Real kindness respects what others truly want, not what we think they need.

slides.inSimpleWords: The story teaches us to listen to all creatures and act with real compassion.

image.alt: What We Learned — Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle

subject: English
title: A Funny Man
hook: A man makes the whole village laugh, but his own heart is breaking. What is the price of making others happy?

characters.name: Gopal
characters.role: the village jester with a tragic secret

characters.name: Sunanda
characters.role: a perceptive girl who sees through the laughter

characters.name: The village
characters.role: the audience that loves his jokes but not the man

slides.title: A Funny Man
slides.storyContext: Laughter hides pain. A comedian's smile may be masking tears.

image.alt: A Funny Man — A Funny Man

slides.title: The Jester's Mask
slides.storyContext: In every village, there's someone like Gopal. He arrives at festivals in a bright turban, tells jokes that make even the oldest men laugh, trips over his own feet, and makes children giggle. The village loves him. But Sunanda, who delivers milk to homes at dawn, sometimes sees Gopal sitting alone by the well, staring at nothing. His face is different then—sad, old, empty. She never mentions it. Then one day, his wife comes to Sunanda's mother asking for work. 'My husband hasn't earned in months. I fear he's falling ill.' Sunanda begins to understand.
slides.inSimpleWords: A funny man hides a sad life beneath his laughter.

image.alt: The Jester's Mask — A Funny Man

slides.title: Irony: When Reality Contradicts Expectation

points.label: What is it?
points.text: When what actually happens is the opposite of what we'd expect. A funny man with a sad life is ironic.

points.label: Why use it?
points.text: Irony creates surprise and makes us think. We assumed Gopal's happiness was real. The shock makes the lesson stick.

example.problem: Everyone thinks Gopal is happy because he makes them laugh. But he's sad. What's ironic?
example.solution: We expect people who bring joy to feel joy themselves. Gopal does the opposite—he sacrifices his own happiness to create happiness for others. The irony makes us question: Does making others laugh mean someone is happy? No.

slides.inSimpleWords: When reality is the opposite of what we expect, that's irony.

image.alt: Irony: When Reality Contradicts Expectation — A Funny Man

slides.title: Tone: The Author's Attitude

points.label: What is tone?
points.text: How the author FEELS about the subject—is it funny? Sad? Angry? Respectful? Mocking?

points.label: In 'A Funny Man'
points.text: At first the tone is light and amused (Gopal's jokes). But it gradually becomes sad and sympathetic (his real life). This shift prepares us for the truth.

example.problem: If the author told only Gopal's jokes, the story would be one tone. If only his sad moments, another. What does mixing them do?
example.solution: Mixing tones forces us to feel both joy and sorrow. We laugh WITH Gopal at first, then laugh AT him along with the village. Then we feel guilty—we never saw his pain. This emotional journey teaches empathy.

slides.inSimpleWords: The author's feeling about the subject shapes how we feel when reading.

image.alt: Tone: The Author's Attitude — A Funny Man

slides.title: Theme: What Does It Mean?

points.label: Possible themes
points.text: 1. 'Appearances deceive—don't judge by surface' 2. 'Kindness is often born of suffering' 3. 'The world needs laughter, but it shouldn't ignore the hurting ones who give it.'

points.label: How to find it
points.text: Look at what the character learns, what changes, and what the author seems to value or critique.

example.problem: What is the main theme of 'A Funny Man'?
example.solution: Likely answer: We often ignore the suffering of those who serve us. Gopal brings joy to earn a living, but the village sees only the performance, not the performer. The theme is about real attention and respect beyond surface appearances.

slides.inSimpleWords: The big life lesson or truth the author is teaching through the story.

image.alt: Theme: What Does It Mean? — A Funny Man

slides.title: Characterization: Showing vs. Telling

points.label: Telling
points.text: 'Gopal was sad inside.' (We're told, but don't feel it.)

points.label: Showing
points.text: 'Sunanda found Gopal at the well at dawn, staring at his reflection. He didn't move for an hour. When he saw her, he startled and put on his bright turban.' (We see his sadness through action.)

points.label: Which is stronger?
points.text: Showing. We trust what we witness over what we're told.

example.problem: The story doesn't say Gopal is in financial trouble. How do we learn it?
example.solution: Through Sunanda's mother, and by observing how his daily choices change—fewer performances, less energy, asking for small loans. The author shows us, not tells us. That's why we believe it and feel for him.

slides.inSimpleWords: Show, don't tell: prove a character's feelings through what they do and say.

image.alt: Characterization: Showing vs. Telling — A Funny Man

slides.title: Empathy Through Understanding

points.label: What Sunanda does
points.text: She doesn't pity Gopal or feel sorry for him. She watches, listens, and understands that his jokes are a job, not his real self.

points.label: Real empathy
points.text: Isn't feeling bad for someone—it's understanding their full humanity and respecting their struggle without judgment.

example.problem: When Sunanda learns about Gopal's wife working for food, does she tell the village?
example.solution: No. Real empathy respects someone's dignity. She might help quietly, or simply greet him with recognition of his real self, not just applause for his jokes. That dignity is worth more than charity.

slides.inSimpleWords: True empathy means seeing someone's whole self, not just their public face.

image.alt: Empathy Through Understanding — A Funny Man

slides.title: The Turning Point: A Simple Moment
slides.storyContext: At the next festival, Gopal is too weak to perform well. His jokes fall flat. Children sense something is wrong. But Sunanda walks up and sits beside him. Without speaking, she holds out a piece of jaggery—not charity, just an offering between friends. The village watches, confused. Gopal's eyes water. Later, the village elder approaches him: 'We laughed at your jokes. We never asked why you needed them so badly. That was unkind of us. Let us help you find steady work.' For the first time in years, Gopal doesn't perform. He simply cries.

example.problem: Why does Sunanda's small gesture matter more than all the village's laughter?
example.solution: Because it's genuine. All the laughter was conditional—'Gopal, be funny for us.' Sunanda's gesture says, 'I see you as a person, not a performer. You matter whether or not you make us laugh.' That recognition is what he's been missing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real recognition heals more than applause ever could.

image.alt: The Turning Point: A Simple Moment — A Funny Man

slides.title: The Mask We Wear
slides.storyContext: Everyone has a public face and a private face. Think about someone in your life who always seems happy (a parent, teacher, friend, relative). Write a short reflection: What might they hide? What might they need recognition for beyond their role?

example.problem: Describe someone's hidden self in 3-4 sentences.
example.solution: Example: 'My mother is always busy, always solving problems for others, always smiling. But sometimes I see her staring out the window. I think she's tired and lonely. She gives so much that nobody asks what she needs. I want her to know that I see HER, not just what she does for us.' (Any thoughtful reflection showing empathy and awareness that people have private struggles is correct.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Consider the private struggles of someone you see every day.

image.alt: The Mask We Wear — A Funny Man

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: **Irony teaches by surprise**: When reality contradicts expectation, we remember the lesson.
**Tone shapes feeling**: How the author feels about the subject influences how we feel.
**Theme is the big truth**: The lesson about life that the story is teaching.
**Show, don't tell**: Prove character through actions, not explanation.
**Real empathy sees the whole person**: Not just their role or what they do for us.
**Recognition heals**: Sometimes people need to be seen, not just used.

slides.inSimpleWords: The story teaches us to look beyond someone's public face and see their real struggle.

image.alt: What We Learned — A Funny Man
